Ingredient: Propylparaben (also known as: Propyl 4-hydroxy­benzoate)
Source: SCCS Opinion on Propylparaben (SCCS/1623/20), SCCS opinion, conclusion
Status: assessed
Scientific opinion: The SCCS considers Propylparaben safe for use as a preservative in cosmetic products at concentrations up to 0.14%. Although available data indicate potential endocrine effects, the evidence is insufficient to classify Propylparaben as an endocrine-disrupting substance or to establish a risk assessment threshold based on such effects. Environmental safety was not assessed.

Ingredient: ZINC PYRITHIONE (also known as: Pyrithione zinc, ZPT, 13463-41-7, 236-671-3)
Source: SCCS Opinion on Zinc pyrithione (SCCS/1614/19), SCCS/1614/19, Final Opinion on Zinc Pyrithione (ZPT), submission III, p. 25
Status: assessed
Conditions: Applies to rinse-off hair products used as anti-dandruff products. Maximum concentration assessed: 1%. The assessment takes overall exposure from other sources into account. The opinion reports no further scientific concerns in response to the second question and no minority opinion.
Hazard classification: The SCCS assessed the safety of Zinc Pyrithione as an anti-dandruff ingredient in rinse-off hair products, taking into account the overall exposure from other sources.
Scientific opinion: The SCCS considers Zinc Pyrithione safe when used as an anti-dandruff ingredient in rinse-off hair products at a maximum concentration of 1%, under the conditions assessed.
Source wording: In line with the conditions laid out in Article 15(d) (i.e. ‘overall exposure from other sources’) of the Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and taking into account the scientific data provided, the SCCS considers Zinc Pyrithione (ZPT) as safe when used as an anti-dandruff in rinse-off hair products up to a maximum concentration of 1%.
payload.section: SCCS/1614/19, Final Opinion on Zinc Pyrithione (ZPT), submission III, p. 25

payload.text:
Ingredient: HOMOSALATE (also known as: Benzoic acid, 2-hydroxy-, 3,3,5-trimethylcyclohexyl ester)
Source: SCCS Opinion on Homosalate (SCCS/1622/20), SCCS/1622/20, Final Opinion on Homosalate (p. 52)
Status: assessed
Conditions: Homosalate is considered safe as a UV filter up to a maximum concentration of 0.5% in the final cosmetic product. Exposure from products outside the scope of the opinion and combined exposure to salicylic acid or other salicylates were not considered. The efficacy of homosalate at lower concentrations was outside the SCCS remit.
Hazard classification: The SCCS identified concerns regarding the potential endocrine-disrupting properties of homosalate. The available evidence from in silico modelling, in vitro tests, and in vivo studies was considered inconclusive and insufficient to establish a specific endocrine-related toxicological point of departure for safety assessment.
Scientific opinion: Homosalate is not considered safe as a UV filter in cosmetic products at concentrations up to 10%. The SCCS considers it safe for consumers only up to a maximum concentration of 0.5% in the final product. Although some studies suggest potential endocrine effects, the current evidence is inconclusive. Further considerations include exposure from other products and combined exposure to salicylic acid and other salicylates, which were not assessed.
Source wording: In the SCCS’s opinion, the use of homosalate as a UV filter in cosmetic products is safe for the consumer up to a maximum concentration of 0.5% homosalate in the final product.

payload.text:
Ingredient: BENZOPHENONE-3 (also known as: 2-Hydroxy-4-methoxybenzophenone)
Source: SCCS Opinion on Benzophenone-3 (SCCS/1625/20), SCCS/1625/20, Overall safety assessment of benzophenone-3 (p. 82)
Status: assessed
Conditions: BP-3 is considered safe up to 6% as a UV filter in face creams, hand creams, and lipsticks, and up to 0.5% when used to protect cosmetic formulations. In body creams, propellant sprays, and pump sprays, the maximum safe UV-filter concentration is 2.2%, provided that no additional 0.5% is used to protect the formulation. If BP-3 is also used at 0.5% for formulation protection, the UV-filter concentration should not exceed 1.7%.
Hazard classification: The SCCS identified concerns regarding the potential endocrine-disrupting properties of benzophenone-3 (BP-3). The available evidence from in silico modelling, in vitro tests, and in vivo studies was considered inconclusive. The assessment also identified safety concerns associated with the use of BP-3 at 6% as a UV filter in body creams and sunscreen sprays.
Scientific opinion: Benzophenone-3 can be considered safe under specific conditions of use, depending on the cosmetic product and concentration. The SCCS considers its use as a UV filter up to 6% safe in face creams, hand creams, and lipsticks, but not in body creams or sunscreen sprays at that concentration. For body creams and sunscreen sprays, the maximum safe concentration is 2.2% when BP-3 is used only as a UV filter, or 1.7% when an additional 0.5% is used to protect the cosmetic formulation. Although the evidence does not conclusively establish BP-3 as an endocrine-disrupting substance, further investigation is warranted. Environmental safety was not assessed.
Source wording: The use of BP-3 as a UV-filter up to a maximum concentration of 6% in sunscreen products, either in the form of body cream, sunscreen propellant spray or pump spray, is not safe for the consumer.
payload.section: SCCS/1625/20, Overall safety assessment of benzophenone-3 (p. 82)

Ingredient: RETINOL; RETINYL ACETATE; RETINYL PALMITATE (also known as: Vitamin A, Retinol, Retinyl Acetate, Retinyl Palmitate)
Source: SCCS Opinion on Vitamin A (SCCS/1576/16), SCCS/1576/16, Final Opinion on Vitamin A (Retinol, Retinyl Acetate and Retinyl Palmitate) and Corrigendum (pp. 69–70)
Status: assessed
Conditions: Maximum concentrations assessed are 0.05% Retinol Equivalent (RE) in body lotions and 0.3% RE in other leave-on and rinse-off products, subject to the applicable regulatory restrictions. The SCCS considered 1500 μg RE/day for adults and children above 6 years and 800 μg RE/day for children aged 1–3 years when assessing systemic exposure. Exposure from dietary supplements was not included. Vitamin A-containing sunscreen products and exposure in children under 1 year were not assessed. Retinoic acid must not be present except as an unavoidable trace impurity with a justified limit, and retinol formulations require adequate stabilisation.
Hazard classification: The SCCS identified teratogenic potential, liver toxicity, and local skin effects as critical toxicological endpoints for vitamin A. Dietary exposure may already approach the tolerable upper intake level (UL), meaning additional exposure from cosmetics could exceed it. Data gaps remain regarding impurities, product stability, and exposure from dietary supplements and certain vitamin A derivatives.
Scientific opinion: The SCCS considers retinol, retinyl acetate, and retinyl palmitate safe at the maximum notified concentrations in the assessed cosmetic product categories, including for children above 1 year under the evaluated conditions. However, total vitamin A exposure from diet, supplements, and cosmetics is an important concern, particularly for susceptible groups. The assessment does not cover sunscreen products, children under 1 year, retinyl linoleate, or retinal. Manufacturers should ensure product stability and control impurities, particularly retinoic acid.
Source wording: Based on these estimates, the SCCS considers that the use of Vitamin A in the respective cosmetic products at the maximum notified concentration per se is safe for children above 1 year old.
payload.section: SCCS/1576/16, Final Opinion on Vitamin A (Retinol, Retinyl Acetate and Retinyl Palmitate) and Corrigendum (pp. 69–70)

payload.text:
Ingredient: SALICYLIC ACID (also known as: Benzoic acid, 2-hydroxy-, 69-72-7, 200-712-3)
Source: SCCS Opinion on Salicylic acid (SCCS/1646/22), SCCS/1646/22, Final Opinion on Salicylic Acid (pp. 54–55)
Status: assessed
Conditions: Maximum concentrations are 0.5% as a preservative, 3.0% for rinse-off hair products, 2.0% for other eligible products, and 0.5% for body lotions, eye shadow, mascara, eyeliner, lipstick, oral products, and non-spray deodorants. Not applicable to sprayable products that may lead to lung exposure by inhalation. Salicylic acid is not permitted in products for children under 3 years of age. The assessment applies to salicylic acid only, not other salicylates or salicylic acid salts.
Hazard classification: The SCCS identified salicylic acid as an eye irritant with the potential to cause serious eye damage. Safety concerns were also noted for children aged 3–10 years due to the absence of exposure data for this age group.
Scientific opinion: The SCCS considers salicylic acid safe as a preservative at concentrations up to 0.5% under the current restrictions. For other cosmetic purposes, it is considered safe up to 3.0% in rinse-off hair products, 2.0% in other eligible products, and 0.5% in body lotions, eye makeup, lipstick, oral products, and non-spray deodorants. These conclusions do not apply to sprayable products that may expose the lungs through inhalation. Further caution is warranted for children aged 3–10 years because exposure data are lacking.
Source wording: The SCCS is of the opinion that salicylic acid (CAS 69-72-7) is safe when used as preservative at a concentration of 0.5 % in cosmetic products, considering its current restrictions in place.
payload.section: SCCS/1646/22, Final Opinion on Salicylic Acid (pp. 54–55)

payload.text:
Ingredient: BUTYLATED HYDROXYTOLUENE (also known as: 2,6-Di-Tert-Butyl-4-Methylphenol, BHT)
Source: SCCS Opinion on BHT (SCCS/1636/21), SCCS/1636/21 Opinion on Butylated Hydroxytoluene (BHT), Conclusion p. 26
Status: assessed
Conditions: BHT is considered safe up to 0.001% in mouthwash, 0.1% in toothpaste, and 0.8% in other leave-on and rinse-off products, including combined use at these concentrations.
Hazard classification: The SCCS assessed BHT in light of concerns regarding its potential endocrine-disrupting properties. Environmental safety was not assessed because environmental aspects fall outside the SCCS mandate.
Scientific opinion: The SCCS considers BHT safe for use in mouthwash at concentrations up to 0.001%, in toothpaste up to 0.1%, and in other leave-on and rinse-off cosmetic products up to 0.8%. BHT is also considered safe when these product categories are used in combination at their respective maximum concentrations. The assessment does not cover environmental safety.
Source wording: BHT is also considered safe for a combined use of mouthwash at a concentration of 0.001%, toothpaste at a concentration of 0.1% and other leave-on and rinse-off products at the concentration of 0.8%.
payload.section: SCCS/1636/21 Opinion on Butylated Hydroxytoluene (BHT), Conclusion p. 26

payload.text:
Ingredient: OCTOCRYLENE (also known as: 2-Cyano-3,3-diphenyl acrylic acid 2-ethylhexyl ester)
Source: SCCS Opinion on Octocrylene (SCCS/1627/21), SCCS/1627/21, Final Opinion on Octocrylene (p. 44)
Status: assessed
Conditions: Octocrylene is considered safe up to 10% as a UV filter when used individually. For combined use involving sunscreen propellant spray and face cream, hand cream, and lipstick containing 10% Octocrylene, the concentration in the propellant spray should not exceed 9%. Benzophenone, as an impurity and/or degradation product, should be kept at trace level. Exposure from products outside the scope of the SCCS opinion was not considered.
Hazard classification: The SCCS identified indications from some in vivo studies of potential endocrine effects, but the evidence was insufficient to establish a specific endocrine-related toxicological point of departure. Contact sensitisation has been reported, although reported cases of allergic contact dermatitis appear negligible relative to widespread use. Photoallergy is strongly associated with previous photoallergy to topical ketoprofen.
Scientific opinion: The SCCS considers Octocrylene safe as a UV filter at concentrations up to 10% when used individually and for specified combinations of sunscreen cream or lotion, pump spray, face cream, hand cream, and lipstick. However, 10% or higher in sunscreen propellant sprays is not considered safe when used in combination with other Octocrylene-containing products. For combined use with face cream, hand cream, and lipstick containing 10% Octocrylene, the concentration in sunscreen propellant spray should not exceed 9%. Although evidence of potential endocrine effects remains inconclusive, further research may be warranted. Environmental safety was not assessed.
Source wording: The use of Octocrylene in sunscreen propellant spray is considered safe when its concentration does not exceed 9% when used together with face cream, hand cream, and lipstick containing 10% Octocrylene.

Ingredient: Phenoxyethanol (also known as: 2-phenoxyethanol)
Source: SCCS Opinion on Phenoxyethanol (SCCS/1575/16), SCCS/1575/16, Overall safety assessment of 2-phenoxyethanol (p. 82)
Status: assessed
Conditions: Assessment is based on dermal exposure and aggregate exposure to preservatives in cosmetics. The concentration limit is not stated in this excerpt.
Hazard classification: Haematotoxicity is described as a predominant toxicological feature of 2-phenoxyethanol in vivo and in vitro. Rabbits were the most sensitive species tested. The main metabolite, 2-phenoxyacetic acid, may accumulate in the kidney and may be responsible for kidney toxicity in rats after oral exposure.
Scientific opinion: Using an adjusted NOAEL of 357 mg/kg bw/day from a 90-day dermal study in rabbits and aggregate exposure for preservatives in cosmetics, a Margin of Safety (MoS) of 130 was derived for adults, against a minimum MoS of 25 selected by the SCCS. The SCCS states this span also covers the safety of infants and babies. For children up to 3 years, exposure may be higher than for adults, but MoS values from reasonable worst-case scenarios are considered sufficient (e.g. MoS of 41 with the EFSA 7 kg default body weight).
Source wording: Using an adjusted NOAEL of 357 mg/kg bw/day from a 90-day dermal RDT study in rabbits and the aggregate exposure for preservatives in cosmetics, for adult humans a MoS of 130 was derived.

Ingredient: TITANIUM DIOXIDE (NANO) (also known as: Titanium dioxide (nano), Eclipse 70, 13463-67-7, 1317-70-0, 1317-80-2)
Source: SCCS Opinion on Titanium dioxide (nano) coating (SCCS/1667/24), SCCS/1667/24, Final Opinion on New Coating for Titanium Dioxide (Nano Form) (p. 44)
Status: assessed
Conditions: Safety could not be established for Eclipse 70 based on the submitted information. Additional data on physicochemical properties, coating stability, dermal absorption, toxicology, and exposure are needed. The general Annex VI concentration limit is 25% for titanium dioxide and titanium dioxide (nano) combined.
Hazard classification: The SCCS identified uncertainties and data gaps concerning titanium dioxide (nano) coated with 6% Aluminium Hydroxide, 14% Sodium Myristoyl Sarcosinate, and 10% Dimethicone (Eclipse 70). The available information did not establish similarity to previously assessed titanium dioxide nanomaterials regarding physicochemical characteristics, coating stability, or lack of dermal absorption.
Scientific opinion: The SCCS could not conclude that titanium dioxide (nano) coated with 6% Aluminium Hydroxide, 14% Sodium Myristoyl Sarcosinate, and 10% Dimethicone (Eclipse 70) is safe for use as a UV filter in dermally applied cosmetic products. Further physicochemical, toxicological, and exposure data specific to this nanomaterial are needed to resolve the identified uncertainties. This conclusion concerns the specific coated material assessed and should not be interpreted as a general finding that all forms of titanium dioxide (nano) are unsafe.
Source wording: Considering all the provided information, the SCCS is of the view that there are a number of uncertainties and data gaps that do not allow a conclusion on the safety of titanium dioxide (nano) coated with a combination of w/w 6% Aluminium Hydroxide, 14% Sodium Myristoyl Sarcosinate and 10% Dimethicone (Eclipse 70).
payload.source: SCCS Opinion on Titanium dioxide (nano) coating (SCCS/1667/24)
payload.section: SCCS/1667/24, Final Opinion on New Coating for Titanium Dioxide (Nano Form) (p. 44)
